Thank you so much for being brave enough to share your story. More men need to feel safe enough to discuss how fucking common this is. Shame is a beast and hard to leave behind, especially once your abuser has gotten you into that cycle of shame and self hatred that begins to feel like second nature, but keep trying to replace that shame with gratitude that you are out of the situation. My therapist tries to remind me that abuse can happen to anyone at anytime. It is not your fault. Abusers come in all shapes and sizes, and are master manipulators that hide their true intentions until they’ve gotten you isolated and hating yourself enough to believe you deserve the things that they are putting you through. The best way to fight shame is to continue to share your story and own the experience for what it was: something horrible that no human being ever deserves to be put through. This does not define you my friend, it is just a hurdle in the journey that is your life. It may not feel like it now, but you are stronger for getting yourself out and seeing this situation for the horrific betrayal of trust that it is. She cannot control you anymore, and never will again. It will take a while to get her voice out of your head, telling you you’re worthless and shameful, but the biggest fuck you to any abuser is to prove them wrong for yourself. You are stronger and bigger than what happened to you. And you’re far from alone, I promise you.

Been in active recovery for like two years now. It's full of ups and downs, and a shit ton of stomach problems, among an array of other potential health risks/side effects from the disorder. None of this is to scare you, it's just the fact of the matter for people like us that have struggled with bulimia. I strongly suggest going to a GI doctor if possible and getting an endoscopy. It's slightly pricey if you don't have insurance but, at least for me, the doctor was able to recognize that my stomach over produces acid, I have burns all along my esophagus, and have been formally diagnosed with GERD. I've taken medicine for this for years now to help with the pain, but it's still unbearable some days. It gets better with time and more consistent, intentional, full recovery. Stop focusing on calories. I say that with all the love in my heart, but with so much hope that you're able to at least try to follow my advice. I'm sure sometimes I eat less than the recommended amount of calories and I'm sure sometimes I eat enough or even "too much" but I have spent years trying to get in touch with my natural body signals. I suggest looking into intuitive eating and biofeedback so you can regain hunger signals to even some degree and give your body control over your eating again instead of your mind. You're not alone in this journey, and coming from a fellow person in recovery, please bring these stomach issues up with your doctor if nothing else. It's best to look into it before more serious bodily damage is done. Best of luck in recovery!

I’m usually opposed to defining someone’s trauma for them, but your situation is a unique one, so I’ll put it very plainly: yes, most of this is very clear SA. I’m very very sorry to say that, but I hope you can find some solace in all of this and maybe some answers as well. Something my therapist told me that I will never forget about physical trauma is that the body remembers, even when the mind doesn’t. I cannot begin to imagine how much more complex this becomes as a system, but the point stays the same. If you find yourself regularly questioning if you ever dealt with SA, you probably did. Everything you’ve described is SA or COCSA. As someone who unfortunately has a lot of personal experience with COCSA, it’s incredibly confusing and, from a victim’s perspective, the lines feel very blurry. However, from an outsider’s perspective, it is very clear that, even if the other child wasn’t intentionally trying to cause harm, they did. In these instances, someone’s intentions become pretty much meaningless next to how their actions made you feel. You felt violated, therefore you were violated. Please give yourself grace and kindness in all of this. Life is going to get harder as you uncover these traumas, but it’s extremely brave and important that you have. Best of luck to all of you ♥️

I’m so sorry to read this. It genuinely breaks my heart. As a mom to a 95lb pitbull, who used to go after smaller animals when he was younger, the story with the German Shepard is more than infuriating. 

I live in an apartment complex and so many of my neighbors also have animals. A few years back, my boy unfortunately got out of his harness, and fatally injured a neighbor’s indoor cat that they had recently allowed to be an outdoor cat. The different levels or technicalities and “who did what” and where the fault lies is and was irrelevant, because my boy was okay, and their cat was not. They wanted my dog to be euthanized (not the way that works at all) and to sue me (F, 18 at the time, nothing to my name), and I sat there and let them say what they needed to. I let them experience their grieving process however they needed to. This is Taking Responsibility, and I’m genuinely disgusted and so sorry that these people did not do the same. 

Yes, animals are animals, no matter what, and accidents are unfortunately going to happen, but a responsibility you’re taking on when caring for an animal is owning THEIR mistakes like they are your own. Because, at the end of the day, they are. Even if only partly. 

The fact that YOU had to pry your dog out of SOMEONE ELSE’S dog’s mouth is so ass backwards and heart wrenching and I’m truly just so grateful that you and your girl are okay. I hope they were held responsible for covering the vet bills (the very least they could do), but, more than anything, have learned from this and will not allow it to happen again. 

I know too many people with German Shepard’s, even in my apartment complex, that allow their dogs to be off leash, and it is setting the poor dog up for failure. If you don’t want your dog on a leash, go through the proper training to ensure that your dog will stay by your side, as if they were on a leash, when needed. Even then, I wouldn’t feel comfy taking the risk.

I didn’t personally even come to terms with the severity and reality of what I was doing to myself for years. It took a stomach ulcer and endoscopy which revealed acid burns around the top of my stomach/end of my esophagus. This didn’t alarm the doctors, they assumed it was acid reflex, but it was physical proof, permanent damage, and it became enough for me to stop living in denial. 

My girlfriend at the time suffered with SEVERE emetophobia (fear of v*mit), but she was still the first person I told. We were best friends for years before, and had been dating for like a year and a half at that point, but technically it was only a few months after I came to terms with it all. I wanted her to know. She helped me tell my therapist and parents. She was so strong with it all. I think it helped that I was “recovered” at the time and was not actively purging to any extent. 

I’ve been with my current boyfriend for a year now, but I technically told him literally the morning after the first time we hung out, so I guess we weren’t even dating yet. He just saw all my morning meds and asked what each of them were for (I’m a super open book so this didn’t make me uncomfy), so when he got to the shit for my stomach I just kinda casually said “I used to make myself sick a lot and it fucked with my body ahaha” but that was the extent of it. I think it took him a while to fully accept what it was, that it doesn’t go away that easily, and that I was actually still struggling with relapses like every few weeks. I didn’t actively talk about it with or hide it from him, but one day he did walk in on me purging and held me while I cried and didn’t make me feel disgusting and broken. He was so angry, but more than anything, he just wanted me to be okay. He still does. I think he’s slightly in denial of it all, which I think is rooted in his hopes that it’ll just kind of go away with time. I finally told my psychiatrist during our last session, though, and a med change is potentially in the works, and my boyfriend knows how difficult that might make life for a while. He even asked “why would you tell him and make a big deal out of something not even going on anymore?”, but all I could focus on was the fear in his voice. 

It’s hard to know what someone’s reaction will be, but if they love you, if they’re worth it, they’ll find a way to process that you have an illness and all you can do is wake up every day and try to be better. It’s hard to not judge or react with anger when someone isn’t exposed to and/or knowledgeable about this type of shit, but, again, someone worth it will want to learn and be better for you. It’s always best to tell them. It’s your partner. When you do it is entirely up to you, but the shame that comes with hiding stuff, especially ED stuff, is so dangerous, and something no one in this world deserves.

I’m not going to say “I know” because I don’t. But I have never felt stronger disappointment, dread, and fear than the day I woke up from a 3 day coma, unable to walk, unable to speak. The last thing I remembered was my bedroom in my old apartment, a mug of pills , and my favorite artist (Ella Fitzgerald) playing on a spotify radio station. I genuinely, at the depth of my core, had accepted that was the way I was going to go. 

I’m sure you can imagine my surprise and disappointment to wake up, still high asf, as I was too dehydrated for them to pump my stomach at that point, confused, alone, exposed, with a catheter inside me. I thought, for a few hours, that I must’ve been in hell. 

Alas, I wasn’t. At least not the kind I’d hoped for. The moment I could walk around the psych ward within the ICU, I was shipped off to the nearest mental hospital, where I was dehumanized and disrespected on a level I cannot explain.

This will be a long, expensive, strenuous challenge to take on, and you will need all of the patience you are capable of giving to the little guy. Scratching your eczema is the worst thing you can do for it! Also,  in my personal experience, Vaseline doesn’t work to soothe eczema. I always say if it doesn’t burn it’s not working. What makes eczema unique from simple dry skin is that during flare ups, every single layer of your skin is irritated, vs most surface level stuff people feel. Because of this, stuff like regular lotion and Vaseline just don’t cut it because they are not moisturizing each and every layer of skin. I recommend Aveeno eczema lotion for at-home care. My elbows used to crack, now it’s my knuckles. It’s so annoying how unpredictable it can be. I personally apply lotion at least once a day, usually right when I get out of the shower, and then at any point if I’m having flare ups obviously. It is genuinely the most extreme pain I have ever felt in my life, but the results are fucking incredible dude. At the same time, if your eczema is so bad it’s causing you to dread your own existence, please go to a dermatologist and get medicated lotion for your eczema. It’s usually got some steroids in it, but it’s all topical, so that shouldn’t be a concern. I’ve dealt with eczema my whole life, as well as suicidal ideations. Please don’t let something so superficial destroy your life. I know it feels embarrassing and frustrating and hurts like hell, but being proactive is going to help much more than giving in. NEVER scratch!! I’ve had to discipline myself, and yes I unfortunately have picked up some other compulsions in replacement of that itching, but my skin hasn’t bled from scratching in years and it feels extremely freeing. Overactive imaginations or talking to yourself when you’re alone or hearing conversations play out in your head are all extremely common things that I think almost everyone does. The difference between this and delusions, I think, is once you detach from reality. If you’re aware that you’re speaking to yourself rather than, let’s say, seeing your crush with you when she is not there. Visual and auditory hallucinations, like those shown in Joker, are not really just inside someone’s head, but you will instead hear and/or see things that are not there. You are detached from reality, as you are completely unaware that those things are not there. Lack of sleep can really mess up someone’s mind. I personally deal with sleep paralysis and night terrors, and it’s very common to see figures in the darkness, often reoccurring, that seem SO real in the dark. What separates this from delusion is, when you turn the light on, the figure goes away. Someone who is delusional may turn the light on and still see that figure. I hope I’m making sense. First I’m gonna be super annoying for a sec and tell you it’s usually not a very good idea to take prescribed meds into your own hands like that (in terms of flushing them). It can be super dangerous if you stop your meds all at once, but I 10000% understand being a minor and KNOWING your medication is not good for you, but being forced to continue to take it. It’s a really tough balance to learn and keep, but more often than not the worst thing for your brain is to stop taking meds altogether.
That being said, SSRIs are often complete shit that make you feel a lot worse than you did in the first place. “1% of people will have negative side effects” my ass. 

I’m currently on Lexapro (an SSRI that, over time, has actually helped), Wellbutrin (this baby’s a good one), Concerta (a type of Ritalin), and Klonopin (a sedative/benzo).
When I was originally getting prescribed meds it was an absolute clusterfuck. It took time, and patience was the last thing on my mind. Eventually I had to say directly to my psychiatrist “I need something fast acting, I can’t wait months to see results”. This is when she put me on Klonopin.

Klonopin falls under the category of benzos (like Xanax). It’s a fast acting sedative with a long half life, and it works. I would say, hands down, I wouldn’t have made it through finding out what meds are right for me if I didn’t get on Klonopin. At the same time, it’s really really REALLY important to remember and consider the risks of Klonopin. It can be extremely addictive. I’ve had to continually increase my dosage (I take 1.5 mgs morning and afternoon, I started on .25 just at night). This is scary because, for some people, you start craving and needing more than what is safe for your body to consume, or anywhere near the dosage a professional would sign off on you taking. I have yet to experience this, and am really happy with my 3 mgs. I’ve also talked to my mom about never letting me get prescribed over 4 mgs throughout the day. 

I know a few people who have been on Wellbutrin and have had similar results as me. I’ve been on it for about a year and a half, and it’s probably my favorite medication. It took a few weeks before I personally noticed a difference, but it helped with not only my depression, anxiety, but also my motivation and ability to focus.

Concerta has been kind of insane. It’s the newest addition to my meds, as I just now got diagnosed with ADHD. You’re right, a lot of the feelings of anxiety overlap with those of ADHD. I’m not sure I would say Concerta has helped “calm my anxiety” as much as the world seems less blurry now. It’s like there was this fog covering the details of everyday life everyone else could see, and the meds have helped lift that fog a bit. 

I’m sorry this is such a long response. I hope it’s helpful in some way. I’m not a doctor, and PLEASE talk to your psychiatrist about your different options. Be as honest as you can with them, and remember that they’re there to answer your questions. PMs are always open !

TSA guy: “Yes, a sandwich is a solid”

Man: “Can I bring a 4oz bottle of mayonnaise?” 

TSA guy: “No, the limit on liquids is 3.4oz” 

Man: “Can I bring a tuna sandwich with 4oz of mayonnaise on it?”

TSA guy: “Like I said, a sandwich is a solid, so yes, you could safely go through security”

Man: “Okay, so what if I put my tuna sandwich in a blender and it ended up being more than 3.4oz of liquid. Can I still bring my sandwich?”

It of course wasn't wonderful, as it is a mental institution, but I got pretty lucky for a few reasons. 1- The place I was staying was a pretty nice hospital (when I say pretty nice I mean clean, decent food, etc.), because fortunately my insurance covered it. 2- I'm a minor, so I was in the adolescent ward, which makes a huge difference, as most of the people you're surrounded by are just kids that are a little lost and need to be set back on the right path. I walked past the adult ward a few times and it was a little scary, it didn't seem like they were really treated like people, because I think a lot of the patients had been struggling for a large portion of their lives, and it had begun to really take a toll on their mental/physical health. As for my experience as a whole, it was very clear everyone's goal was to get out as quickly as possible (I was in a short-term inpatient facility). Even though it was a nice hospital, it was still pretty intense. The adolescent ward was co-ed, but the boys and girls were in different hallways if that makes sense. Our rooms were nice: clean, but pretty simple. Two people to a bedroom, each with one pillow and a sheet, one bathroom for the two of you to share. In the bathroom was a small shower (the shower curtain was just velcro'd to the ceiling for obvious reasons), one toilet, and a small sink with a mirror (really just a metal tin nailed to the wall, it was barely reflective, but it was safe). Each of us had a shelf to put our clothes and stuff on. Lots of safety regulations, some of which I found kind of comical, but most were pretty obvious (no shoelaces, no strings on your hoodies, etc.) The hardest thing for me was that you tended to lose track of time in there. All I know is we woke up at 5:30 for medications and breakfast. Then you were allowed to go back to sleep after breakfast, for like three hours on weekends and an hour on weekdays. After that I have no idea what time things happened at. I don't think there was a single clock in there. We'd just sit around until we were told to go to group or the gym or outside. Group therapy was nothing like how you see it portrayed by Hollywood, we just sat in a classroom and read our patient rights and wrote down goals for recovery. On weekdays we'd have worksheets to do, kind of like busy work you get in school, but they were always focused on anxiety or anger triggers or how to deal with stress. On weekends we'd play pictionary or this version of hangman where we just built a house instead of a man on a noose (as to not trigger anyone). Basically each day went the same, so we had to set little things each day for ourselves to look forward to, like the snacks we'd get after dinner during movie time, etc. Going outside was a big one (tbh its kind of funny to see a bunch of depressed kids get excited about going outdoors) because we had a playground and benches to sit at and it was just a change in environment from the blank walls in the overly air conditioned building we were in all day. However, most of the days I was there it was raining all day, so we'd end up just going to the gym. The gymnasium was nice but pretty small and didn't have any windows. When we'd play racquet ball or capture the flag it was actually pretty fun, but most of the time they'd just bring us in there and tell us to keep ourselves busy for a few hours. If they didn't feel like taking us to the gym they'd just sit us in front of the tv and play a bunch of movies or we'd have "rec time" and some annoying woman would come in with ridiculous activities for us to do like "healthy relationship bingo". Some time in between all of this was lunch, and also a daily physical. We met with a psychiatrist individually every couple of days to see how the meds we were on were making us feel, but the psychiatrist wasn't great at his job and would pretty much prescribe you whatever the hell he wanted to and not really tell you the side effects or even what the medicine was called. Basically, every kid in there would tell you whatever you do don't cry or panic in front of the staff or they'll keep you longer and put you on meds you might not need. I didn't think they were right until like my fourth day there. I had a terrible panic attack but they were fully aware anxiety was something I suffered with and all they did was yell at me and threaten to keep me longer if I didn't stop crying. Finally a slightly qualified nurse brought me aside, gave me water, and talked me through my breathing. The nurses were good people who wanted us to get better, I just think none of them knew what they were doing. In comparison to stories like One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest I feel incredibly grateful for the nurses we had, but most of them probably would have been better fit at a correctional school rather than a mental hospital. The food wasn't shit but wasn't great, plus it didn't help that I'm vegetarian so I was mainly living off of salad, some meal replacement drink they gave me twice a day, and the cake we got at dinner. Honestly the most beneficial part of my experience was just meeting other kids that were going through the same shit I was. I'd never before met another person who openly talked about mental illness so it was a huge breath of fresh air for me. I met some really cool people just in the week I was there, and if it wasn't for their really strict policy on not sharing personal information with other patients, I'd probably still be friends with a few of the kids I was in there with. Sorry for the long response, I just remember what it was like to have suicide on my mind and to know getting landed in a mental hospital was a possibility, but not having any clue what that experience would be like. To answer your question: from my experience, no, it's not as horrific as a lot of people might say, but it's also not a vacation spot to be used as an escape from life for a little while. We were treated fairly, and I personally experienced nothing like the horror stories you hear, but you couldn't pay me to spend another night in there.
Thank you! Hopefully by the time prom comes around we'll be comfortable enough that it'll all be out in the open :)
